source.book: The Art and Science of Technical Analysis
source.author: Adam Grimes

conventions: stop and limit entries mechanized as bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode, sides field says mirrored/same; price-level conditions rejected (shift test) -- all candidates here compare price differences or a bar's price to a level derived from recent bars, never an absolute constant

candidates.name: KeltnerBandCloseOutside
candidates.quote: it showed many bars trading completely outside the Keltner channels (multiplefree bars), a most unusual event.
candidates.description: The bar closes entirely outside the Keltner channel: an EMA of length L plus/minus M times the ATR of length L. A 'free bar' in Grimes's terminology.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > ema(close, emaLength) + bandMult * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: needs an EMA and an ATR

notes: Grimes's Keltner default is a 20-period EMA with bands at 2.25 ATR (confirmed in the book's appendix elsewhere). This is a static close-outside-band state, not a cross event like the existing KeltnerChannelCross rule.

candidates.name: ConsecutiveKeltnerFreeBars
candidates.quote: many bars trading completely outside the Keltner channels (multiple free bars)
candidates.description: At least minFreeBars of the last minFreeBars bars closed outside the Keltner band (G05-01) -- unusual, unsustainable parabolic acceleration.
candidates.pseudocode: count(i = 0..minFreeBars-1, close[i] beyond ema(close, emaLength)[i] +/- bandMult * atr(atrLength)[i]) >= minFreeBars

complexity.reason: cross-bar counter over a short window of the free-bar primitive

notes: 'Multiple free bars' has no book-given count; minFreeBars = 3 is a reasonable default.

candidates.name: ClimaxReversalAfterFreeBars
candidates.quote: This type of price action is unsustainable, and the market collapsed back into the vacuum at D.
candidates.description: After a run of consecutive Keltner free bars (G05-02), the first bar to close back inside the band is a countertrend reversal entry -- the parabolic-exhaustion reversal.
candidates.pseudocode: ConsecutiveKeltnerFreeBars[1] == true AND close[0] <= ema(close, emaLength) + bandMult * atr(atrLength)
candidates.book_order_type: stop/market on the close back inside the band -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: builds on the free-bar counter

notes: This is Grimes's parabolic blow-off reversal in Figure 5.12 (Wheat futures).

candidates.name: BarRangeExpansionAtBreakout
candidates.quote: we need to see increased volume, activity, and interest associated with the actual breakout... the quantitative measures that will be most useful will be instantaneous measures of volatility such as the ratio of the current bar's range to a window of previous bars.
candidates.description: The breakout bar's range (high-low) exceeds a multiple of the average range of the preceding N bars -- confirms a volatile, well-supported breakout.
candidates.pseudocode: (high[0] - low[0]) > rangeMultiple * average(high[1..lookback] - low[1..lookback])

complexity.reason: window average of bar range

candidates.name: BreakoutVolumeAboveAverage
candidates.quote: we need to see increased volume, activity, and interest associated with the actual breakout.
candidates.description: Volume on the breakout bar exceeds a multiple of its own N-bar average volume.
candidates.pseudocode: volume[0] > volMultiple * average(volume, lookback)

complexity.reason: window average of volume

candidates.name: TightRangeNearLargerRangeExtreme
candidates.quote: a tight range near the edge of a larger, established trading range. This tight range is often less than 25 percent of the height of the larger range.
candidates.description: The height of a short recent window is less than a fraction of the height of a longer prior window, and that short window sits near the top (long) / bottom (short) of the longer window -- prebreakout accumulation base.
candidates.pseudocode: tightHigh = highest(high, tightLookback); tightLow = lowest(low, tightLookback); rangeHigh = highest(high, rangeLookback); rangeLow = lowest(low, rangeLookback); (tightHigh - tightLow) < tightFraction * (rangeHigh - rangeLow) AND (rangeHigh - tightHigh) < proximityFraction * (rangeHigh - rangeLow)

complexity.reason: two window highest/lowest comparisons, no pivots

notes: 25% is the book's own figure for the tight range's height relative to the larger range; proximityFraction has no stated number, default chosen.

candidates.name: ShrinkingPullbacksIntoResistance
candidates.quote: prices holding higher lows into a more or less clearly defined resistance level... the declines will become shallower simply because more people are buying them.
candidates.description: Each successive pullback low within a trading range is higher than the prior pullback low while the range high stays roughly flat -- an ascending-triangle accumulation pattern preceding a good breakout.
candidates.pseudocode: swingLow[0] > swingLow[1] > swingLow[2] AND abs(swingHigh[0] - swingHigh[1]) < flatTolerance * avgRange AND abs(swingHigh[1] - swingHigh[2]) < flatTolerance * avgRange

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and multi-leg comparison

notes: Grimes gives no exact swing count for the 'ascending triangle' quality; 3 is a reasonable default.

candidates.name: SpringAtRangeSupport
candidates.quote: Violations of support and resistance in well-defined ranges are important areas to watch. If excursions beyond the range are short-lived, printing springs and upthrusts at the edges of the range, this becomes strong evidence that large traders are positioning.
candidates.description: A Wyckoff spring: the bar's low trades below the recent range's support (lowest low of the prior N bars) but the bar closes back above that support level. Mirrored as an upthrust at resistance for shorts. Reused as a primitive by several later candidates in this file.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] < lowest(low[1], rangeLookback) AND close[0] > lowest(low[1], rangeLookback)
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (close-based pattern, no order placement of its own)

complexity.reason: window low plus a close comparison

notes: Shared primitive, first defined here; also used by G05-26 (last gasp).

candidates.name: BeyondLevelBriefExcursion
candidates.quote: a rule of thumb might be that you want to see no more than two or three bars on your time frame outside the breakout level and then strong momentum reversing the move.
candidates.description: No more than maxBarsBeyond consecutive bars have closed beyond a significant level -- a running count since the level was first breached.
candidates.pseudocode: barsBeyondLevel <= maxBarsBeyond, where barsBeyondLevel counts consecutive bars with close[i] on the far side of level

complexity.reason: cross-bar persistent counter

notes: Shared primitive; composes into G05-11 (failure test of a level).

candidates.name: CloseBackWithStrongReversalMomentum
candidates.quote: once a bar closes back on the other side of the breakout level, strong momentum steps in and we see good price rejection from the breakout level.
candidates.description: The bar that closes back on the origin side of a broken level has a body at least a multiple of the recent average range -- a strong reversal/rejection bar.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(close[0] - open[0]) > bodyMultiple * average(high[1..lookback] - low[1..lookback])

complexity.reason: single-bar body vs. window-average range

candidates.name: FailureTestOfLevel
candidates.quote: As a pure price pattern, a failure test is a brief excursion beyond a level, followed by an immediate reversal.
candidates.description: Composite failure test: a brief excursion beyond a level (G05-09) that closes back across the level on a strong-momentum bar (G05-10). Enter against the excursion direction on the close of that bar.
candidates.pseudocode: G05-09 AND G05-10 AND close[0] crosses back to the origin side of level
candidates.book_order_type: market/stop entry on the close of the reversal bar -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: combines two moderate/simple primitives

notes: Also called the 'turkey shoot' in the text (page 146).

candidates.name: WeakFailureTestLowConviction
candidates.quote: lower time frame price action shows a lack of conviction beyond the breakout level... a market that may be holding at higher levels without strong underlying conviction.
candidates.description: A weaker variant of the failure test: the bar closes very near the level with a small body relative to its range (instead of a strong reversal bar). Flagged as a lower-confidence context that still warns of failure momentum within the next several bars.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(close[0] - level) < nearFraction * (high[0] - low[0]) AND abs(close[0] - open[0]) < bodyMultiple * average(high[1..lookback] - low[1..lookback])

complexity.reason: 'lack of conviction' is a qualitative lower-time-frame read; here approximated by a single-bar proxy on the trading time frame

candidates.name: PullbackHoldsOutsideBreakoutLevel
candidates.quote: The market breaks through the level, trades sharply beyond the level, and then makes a clean pullback that holds outside the breakout level.
candidates.description: Since the breakout entry, every bar's low (long) / high (short) has stayed beyond the breakout level, never trading back across it -- the cleanest, easiest-to-manage first pullback.
candidates.pseudocode: lowest(low, ctx.BarsSinceEntry()) > breakoutLevel

complexity.reason: needs the breakout level carried as position state and a since-entry window

candidates.name: StrongMomentumConfirmsBreakoutPullbackContinuation
candidates.quote: It is far more common to see these pullbacks fail with very strong momentum out of the pattern or fail on a second test of the extreme reached after the pullback.
candidates.description: The pullback following a breakout resolves with a strong-momentum bar in the breakout direction (large body relative to recent average range) -- confirms trend continuation and re-entry.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > close[1] AND (close[0] - open[0]) > bodyMultiple * average(high[1..lookback] - low[1..lookback])
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context test) or entry on the close of this bar -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: single-bar body vs. window-average range

candidates.name: SharpCountertrendBreaksBreakoutPullback
candidates.quote: C marks a classic breakout pullback failure, as sharp downside momentum breaks out of the bottom of the pullback.
candidates.description: Point C: within the post-breakout pullback, a bar breaks below the pullback's own low so far with strong momentum against the breakout direction -- an early warning that the breakout is failing.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] < lowest(low[1], barsSincePullbackStart) AND (open[0] - close[0]) > bodyMultiple * average(high[1..lookback] - low[1..lookback])

complexity.reason: needs the pullback's own start tracked since the breakout

candidates.name: FailurePullbackCountertrendEntry
candidates.quote: Shorting into the pullback at D is a good trade based just on that criterion, but, in this case, it is further motivated by the failure of the breakout level at A.
candidates.description: Point D: after G05-15 fires, the first small pullback in the new (countertrend-to-the-original-breakout) direction is a tradable entry against the failed breakout.
candidates.pseudocode: G05-15[n] fired AND this is the first pullback since bar n against the new (post-failure) direction
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (composite context; actual trigger inherits pullback-entry conventions)

complexity.reason: requires tracking a short-term trend change and detecting its first pullback

notes: This is the same pattern Chapter 6 names the 'Failure Pullback' inside the Failed Breakouts template; recorded independently here per the mining brief.

candidates.name: TrendLegCountCaution
candidates.quote: After many directional pushes (more than three), it is likely that the market needs further consolidation before continuing the trend; the probability of pullback failure becomes higher with each subsequent trend leg.
candidates.description: The count of same-direction trend legs since the last opposite-direction leg exceeds a threshold -- raises the odds the next pullback fails; a caution filter reducing confidence in fresh with-trend pullback entries.
candidates.pseudocode: sameDirectionLegCount > maxLegs

complexity.reason: needs swing-leg counting

candidates.name: PullbackStallsIntoRange
candidates.quote: There is simply no move out of the pullback as prices stabilize around a price level in the pullback itself.
candidates.description: After a trend, the pullback's own range fails to expand for N bars -- its high-low envelope stops making new extremes in either direction -- the pullback is transitioning directly into a trading range rather than resuming the trend.
candidates.pseudocode: highest(high, stallBars) - lowest(low, stallBars) < stallFraction * trendLegRange

complexity.reason: 'trading range' is a design-level concept; this is a range-contraction proxy

candidates.name: FailureTestAtPriorTrendExtreme
candidates.quote: Pullbacks may also fail on a test of the pivot that defines the previous trend extreme.
candidates.description: Same failure-test mechanics as G05-11, but the level tested is the pivot that defined the trend's own prior extreme (a highest-high/lowest-low over the trend's lookback) rather than a breakout level -- ends the trend.
candidates.pseudocode: level = highest(high, trendLookback); BeyondLevelBriefExcursion(level) AND CloseBackWithStrongReversalMomentum
candidates.book_order_type: market/stop entry on the close of the reversal bar -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: reuses the failure-test primitives with a different level source

candidates.name: FailurePullbackSequenceMeasuredMoveTarget
candidates.quote: the move out of the failure pullback often exhausts itself somewhere close to the measured move objective (MMO), thus defining the initial extreme of the new trading range.
candidates.description: Target/expectation for the second (renewed) countertrend leg of a failure-pullback sequence: it tends to exhaust near a measured-move projection -- the length of the first countertrend leg added onto the end of the small pullback that followed it.
candidates.pseudocode: target = pullbackEndPrice +/- (firstLegHigh - firstLegLow)
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (profit target, limit at target level)

complexity.reason: needs leg-length measurement from detected swing points

candidates.name: MomentumDivergenceAtExtremeWarnsFailure
candidates.quote: failed pullbacks are preceded by some form of a momentum divergence.
candidates.description: Momentum (a simple close-vs-N-bars-ago reading, or a fast oscillator) fails to make a new extreme alongside a new price extreme -- a divergence that precedes failed pullbacks.
candidates.pseudocode: high[0] >= highest(high[1], lookback) AND momentumValue[0] < momentumValueAtPriorExtreme

complexity.reason: cross-bar state comparing momentum at two price-extreme bars

candidates.name: HighVolatilityBeforePullbackWarnsFailure
candidates.quote: Other common conditions preceding failed pullbacks are extremely high volatility, indicating possible climax or exhaustion.
candidates.description: ATR is elevated well above its own average immediately before a pullback begins -- a climax/exhaustion warning that raises the odds the pullback fails.
candidates.pseudocode: atr(atrLookback) > atrMultiple * average(atr(atrLookback), avgLookback)

complexity.reason: ATR of an ATR average

candidates.name: AcceleratingTrendLegSteepness
candidates.quote: they last a long time and they accelerate into a steeper trend before the actual expansion. This acceleration can either be a series of ever-steeping trend legs.
candidates.description: Each successive with-trend leg's slope (price change divided by bar count) is steeper than the previous leg's -- a warning sign the market may be primed for a parabolic blow-off.
candidates.pseudocode: legSlope[0] > legSlope[1] > legSlope[2], where legSlope = (legEndPrice - legStartPrice) / legBarCount

complexity.reason: needs swing-leg detection plus a slope comparison across an unspecified number of legs

notes: Related to the existing TrendLineSlopeFlattening rule but in the opposite sense (steepening, not flattening).

candidates.name: TriangleConsolidationAfterOppositeImpulses
candidates.quote: If a market makes a sharp move, followed by an almost equally sharp move in the opposite direction, there is a very high probability of an extended consolidation.
candidates.description: Two consecutive impulse legs of similar magnitude in opposite directions (a sharp move immediately reversed by an almost-equally sharp move) -- blocks new entries, since an extended, low-edge consolidation is likely to follow. Most common after parabolic climaxes.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(leg1Length - leg2Length) < similarityFraction * max(leg1Length, leg2Length) AND sign(leg1) != sign(leg2) AND leg2BarCount <= maxLegBars

complexity.reason: needs swing-leg detection and magnitude comparison

notes: Related to but distinct from ExpandingTrianglePattern -- this is a two-leg contraction test, not an expanding pattern.

candidates.name: ConsolidationDurationBeforeExtremeTest
candidates.quote: the key is that it is preceded by sufficient consolidation to set up the potential for another trend leg up.
candidates.description: A range-bound period of at least minConsolidationBars bars (high-low envelope not expanding) occurs immediately before a spring/upthrust test at the trend extreme -- required for the 'last gasp' pattern to carry its full reliability.
candidates.pseudocode: highest(high, consolidationLookback) - lowest(low, consolidationLookback) < consolidationFraction * priorTrendRange, measured over the consolidationLookback bars immediately preceding the test

complexity.reason: 'sufficient consolidation' is a design-level judgment, mechanized here as a range-contraction proxy

candidates.name: LastGaspSpringUpthrust
candidates.quote: The actual 'last gasp' pattern is nothing more than a Wyckoff upthrust, but the key is that it is preceded by sufficient consolidation to set up the potential for another trend leg up; the pattern draws its power from the failure of that potential.
candidates.description: A spring or upthrust (G05-08) at the extreme of an established trend, occurring only after a sufficiently long consolidation (G05-25) -- a high-reliability trend-termination signal.
candidates.pseudocode: ConsolidationDurationBeforeExtremeTest AND SpringAtRangeSupport
candidates.book_order_type: market/stop entry on the close of the spring/upthrust bar -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: combines a moderate primitive with a research-grade consolidation test

candidates.name: ChangeOfCharacterSwingReversal
candidates.quote: a change of character could be as simple as a downswing that is bigger than the preceding upswing. If this is the first time this has happened in many swings, it is time to carefully monitor the market.
candidates.description: The most recent countertrend swing is larger than the with-trend swing immediately preceding it, and no such reversal has occurred in the last M swings -- flags a possible change of character / trend weakening.
candidates.pseudocode: swingLength[0] > priorSameDirectionSwingLength AND no prior occurrence of this in the last numSwingsLookback swings

complexity.reason: needs swing-leg detection and a lookback over prior swing comparisons

rejected.quote: If a trader is planning on paying a breakout above $20.00 and receives fills at $20.20, this is 20 cents of slippage and can be a significant cost of trading.
rejected.reason: execution/fill-price microstructure the backtest engine does not model (intended vs. actual fill price)

rejected.quote: the breakout trader should receive immediate feedback on whether the trade is right or wrong.
rejected.reason: trader psychology / expectation-setting about feedback timing, not a testable bar-level condition

rejected.quote: Who is buying from them? You got it -- the large players are more than happy to pick up some extra inventory from the nervous short-term players.
rejected.reason: narrative about institutional order-flow motivations; the actual testable derivative (failure test, spring/upthrust) is captured separately

rejected.quote: Whether it is company-specific news, a crop report, or a large-scale economic report, fresh information causes market participants to immediately and dramatically reassess their commitment.
rejected.reason: driven by news/fundamental catalysts the engine does not have

rejected.quote: I sometimes refer to a trading skill I (half) jokingly call 'Hey, that's different.' ... Intuition is useful here.
rejected.reason: pure discretion / intuition with no bar-level test

rejected.quote: Imagine that you are a large player who would like to sell some of your inventory... where will those traders probably put their stops?
rejected.reason: explanatory market-microstructure narrative about stop clustering, not itself a bar-level condition (the resulting failure-test pattern is captured as G05-09/G05-10/G05-11)

rejected.quote: A failed trend reversal, then, could be described as a failed failure pattern... they derive their power from potentially trapped traders who were aggressively anticipating trend reversal.
rejected.reason: restates trend-continuation / failure-test mechanics already captured elsewhere in this file; no new bar-level test given

chapter_summary: Covers the transitions between trends and trading ranges: breakouts (prebreakout accumulation patterns, breakout-quality confirmation, failure tests, and the first-pullback continuation/failure fork), trend termination into a trading range (failed pullbacks, momentum-divergence and trend-leg-count warnings), trend reversal (parabolic climax/exhaustion via Keltner 'free bars', the 'last gasp' spring/upthrust, and triangle consolidations after opposite impulses), and trend continuation without warning (mostly rejected as discretionary or news-driven). Defines the Keltner-band, spring/upthrust, and failure-test primitives that recur through the rest of the book; Chapter 6 redefines its own copies of these same primitives per the mining convention rather than referencing this file's IDs.
